blocks.text: The most important non-specific defence is given by the germ-killer cells of the blood, which patrol the bloodstream and attack and kill microbes. There are three basic kinds: macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells.

items: Macrophages develop from monocytes, a type of white blood cell. A macrophage takes in a bacterium by endocytosis and kills it with its enzymes. Some are fixed in organs such as the lungs, liver, spleen and brain, but most patrol the blood, lymph and interstitial fluid.

Neutrophils, another type of white blood cell, kill pathogens in three ways: phagocytosis; releasing soluble anti-microbial chemicals onto pathogens; and releasing a network of DNA fibres that binds and kills pathogenic bacteria.

blocks.text: Natural killer (NK) cells are a type of T-lymphocytes and are also called cytotoxic T-cells. They do not kill invading microbes; they detect and attack body cells infected with viruses. They release perforins, which insert into the target cell's membrane and form a pore; water rushes in and the cell swells and bursts. They also detect cancer cells and kill them before they can develop into a tumour.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says natural killer cells are a type of T-lymphocyte and are also called cytotoxic T cells. In fact NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate (non-specific) defence, not T cells, and they are not the same as cytotoxic T cells, which belong to the specific immune response (topic 21.3.2).

blocks.alt: A germ-killer cell of blood pressed against a target cell. A granule of perforins opens towards the target, perforins cross the narrow gap, and perforin rings form pores in the cell membrane of the target cell. The target cell's nucleus is below.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.6: Natural killer cell attacking an infected cell (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.6).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Perforins, Germ-Killer cell of blood, Target cell, Pore, Nucleus, Cell membrane of target cell (infected cells).

blocks.title: For information: self-proteins
blocks.text: Patrolling cells do not attack the body's own cells, because all normal cells carry a surface protein marker that identifies them, the self-protein. Germ-killer cells attack only cells that lack such proteins.
